texts: bad: "wraith activity at the Sunken Cove" is read as one particular standing thing and asserted as a fact, so the knowledge base ends up claiming there IS wraith activity at the Cove rather than only "if it increases"; the requests are also left untied to the increase that triggers them. Attaching the place to the verb instead of to the abstract noun keeps the whole condition inside the rule: "Whenever wraith activity increases at the Sunken Cove, a station near the Sunken Cove requests feather rations from the Council."

mixed: the rule fires and each request is tied to its trigger, but "ask the Council for feather rations" puts what is wanted behind a preposition, and the parse files the rations in the plain direct-object slot instead of the "for" slot — so this sentence and your "requests … from the Council" wording store the same fact in two places that will not match each other. Use the verb that takes the rations directly: "Whenever wraith sightings at the Sunken Cove rise, the stations request feather rations from the Council."

good. everything is covered — the Council, the group of requests, and the central feather store as what they are weighed against — and the compound store keeps both its "store" genus and its "central" property.

bad: "stations whose lanterns are drained" comes out with "drained" said of the station's lantern set taken as a single object, a shape no ordinary lantern fact will ever match, so the rule cannot fire on a real station; there is also no supported way to say "all of a station's lanterns" inside a condition. Put the condition on one lantern, in its own clause: "Whenever a lantern at a station is drained, the Council usually prioritizes that station."
